body:
> There was a request for symbolic links support (creating & reading links) in [WICG/file-system-access#377](https://github.com/WICG/file-system-access/issues/377), but it was closed as being risky to OPFS. I'd like to re-open this request again here.

To clarify, the risks here are not to OPFS. The risk is that symlinks can be created in a user directory (outside of OPFS) which points to files within the OPFS, since this would effectively bypass the requirement to run Safe Browsing checks and add the Mark-of-the-Web to any file saved to a user's directory.

> First, fs work seems like it applies beyond OPFS, & fs ought to be able to encompass one of the most common filesystem capabilities. 

This repo only pertains to the OPFS (for now, at least). We could consider supporting symlinks exclusively within the OPFS, but I'm not convinced that provides much value, especially since https://github.com/WICG/file-system-access/issues/377 explicitly wants this to "make working with both a user directory and sandboxed files more seamless together"

Could you explain the use case?

> Could you explain the use case?

I'm trying to write tools to help users deal with git repositories, and there are symlink files in users repos that I need to be able to create on users computers if users are going to have their expected experience. FS gets me most of the way there, but doesn't support this core file type.

> The risk is that symlinks can be created in a user directory (outside of OPFS) which points to files within the OPFS, since this would effectively bypass the requirement to run Safe Browsing checks and add the Mark-of-the-Web to any file saved to a user's directory.

Why not have your OS check the symlinked target too? Are there any web specifications for "mark of the web" anywhere we can build off of or work with to help improve this situation? This feels like a pretty baroque concern that shouldn't impede straightforward progress.

In the case of OPFS, I would expect any symlinks to be virtualised, that is, they wouldn't exist on the underlying filesystem as symlinks. Rather, the user-agent could create a mapping (perhaps implemented through some metadata such as an SQLite table) that causes a symlink to be exposed through the API. It's my understanding that common user-agents already possess a virtualisation layer (mapping OPFS paths to some hashed filename on the underlying FS) to prevent websites from being able to create files with arbitrary (and potentially unsafe) filenames/paths.

In the case of granting access to the underlying FS, then of course the symlinks would be real ones on disk (disregarding that Windows requires Developer Mode enabled in order for non-Administrator processes to create symlinks).

> The risk is that symlinks can be created in a user directory (outside of OPFS) which points to files within the OPFS, since this would effectively bypass the requirement to run Safe Browsing checks and add the Mark-of-the-Web to any file saved to a user's directory.

Am I understanding that the risk here is that a user may give a website permission to access (through the File System API) a portion of their user directory which happens to include their web browser profile, and therefore, the underlying OPFS storage for the website? For example:

- The website uses OPFS to write a malicious file into the OPFS storage, therefore writing to disk a file that lacks any Mark-of-the-Web or safe browsing checks.
- Website calls `window.showDirectoryPicker()` and socially engineers the user to select their home directory (e.g. `C:\Users\TerrorBite`).
- The website, having determined the user's browser, reads `C:\Users\TerrorBite\AppData\Roaming\Mozilla\Firefox\profiles.ini` to determine path to the profile
- The website reads and processes `C:\Users\TerrorBite\AppData\Roaming\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\asdfghjk.default\storage\default\https+++malicious.example\fs\metadata.sqlite` to determine the path to the OPFS file it dropped earlier
- The website creates, somewhere in the user's home directory tree, a symlink at some sensitive location (with attacker-controlled filename) that points to e.g. `C:\Users\TerrorBite\AppData\Roaming\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\asdfghjk.default\storage\default\https+++malicious.example\fs\2U\2U57AYDW4UOSVN2YCILD7GOANBN7SRAZWQXFI5UJRSKQFR4OYVHA`
- This results in, effectively, the creation of a trusted file with attacker-controlled filename and content, with no protections in place.

(all paths in the above are fictitious, but plausible)

My proposed solution here would be to restrict the targets of symlinks to files that DO have the Mark-of-the-Web. This would satisfy most use-cases, such as the Git use-case mentioned above, where the files being symlinked to are presumably other files that the same website has previously written, while preventing any symlinks being created to arbitrary content.

I would also assume that symlinks whose target is a file which the user-agent cannot reach (e.g. outside the directory tree granted by the user's selection) would not be allowed to be created, as that would allow a website to access just about anything it knew the path to.

> (all paths in the above are fictitious, but plausible)

Nope ! These are already not selectable...
https://wicg.github.io/file-system-access/#wellknowndirectory-too-sensitive-or-dangerous

> Could you explain the use case ?

Have dir listing to show user's symlinks ! Like not to be deceptive if the user manage stuff with symlinks...  
Be a complete API...


### Permissions
This doesn't look such difficult, according current spec already manage sensitive UserFS path to be forbidden, and I don't see any way to cross filesystems already...

Spec draft:
- Symlinks can't escape filesystem: OPFS's symlinks should point to a OPFS handle, UserFS's symlink should point to a UserFS handle.
- Reading a symlink: 
    - resolve symlink's underlaying path, but don't provide the path to website, instead provide a FileSystemHandle (with or without permission).
    - target must be in a read granted realm, or throw a NotAllowedError. Let website requestPermission is such case, showing to user in permission UI what is the underlaying path, and applying the same restriction as show[...]Picker method's too-sensitive-or-dangerous filtering.
- Writing a symlink: 
    - method takes a FileSystemHandle (not a path string) for target, so no risk of targeting anything arbitrarily located.
    - destination must be in a readwrite granted realm, or throw a NotAllowedError.
    - target must be in a read granted realm, or throw a NotAllowedError. Let website requestPermission is such case the same way as reading but with readwrite permission.
